utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Ladies and gentlemen, General Galic. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue the cross-examination of Mr. Kovac, I'd like to come back on a few issues that were discussed during the past few days, and one of them is how we should deal with documents in this Court. I'll try to explain to you as clearly as I can how we intend to do it. If there are any questions remaining, you always can ask it to the Registrar, and if there's any problem in relation with that, she'll be in touch with me to solve these problems. So how to deal with documents that have been used during trial. We are talking about documents that have been shown to a witness or have been shown to the Chamber, not just documents of which a few lines have been read without showing them to the Chamber or to the other party or to a witness. It should be clear from the beginning whether the party that shows such a document or an object or a video intends to tender the document in evidence because if it's not intended to have this document tendered in evidence, it will just be marked for identification. The procedure for marking for identification is the following one: One, documents to be marked for identification do not need any pre-numbering by the parties. Two, the original of the document should be handed over to the Registrar. Three, the Registrar marks the document for identification, giving it an MFI number, and signs it. Four, the Registrar will then keep the document for a while, she'll make a copy of the marked original. That copy of the marked original will stay with the Registry. Five, the marked original will be returned to the party that has used the document. A similar procedure is valid as far as videos that are shown are concerned, if they are not tendered into evidence. Then I come to the second category that are documents, objects, videos, et cetera that are tendered in evidence by one of the parties. Pre-numbering by the party on the document concerned is required. So that was rule number 1. Number 2, the intention to tender into evidence the document or video or whatever object should be indicated upon the first use of the document, video, or other object during trial. Three, the other party can then raise immediately any objection, so already upon this indication. If no objection is raised, and that's number 4, the document, video, object, will be tendered into evidence at the end of the examination of the witness by the party. And if it is admitted into evidence, it is given an exhibit number, which will be the number given by the party but then preceded by either a P, for Prosecution, or a D, for Defence. Once the document is admitted into evidence, we will call them exhibits. So until that moment, they are just documents, documents not to be tendered into evidence, or documents just to be identified. But once they are admitted in evidence, they will be referred to as exhibits, and then the number given to it by the Registry. I now come to documents that bear any markings on them, markings made by a witness. If during examination-in-chief the witness has put any markings on a document, first the blank document should be tendered into evidence as well as the marked document. It is suggested to the parties not to tender the marked document in evidence until cross-examination is concluded. If different colours for marking are used during examination-in-chief and during cross-examination - we started yesterday with red for the Prosecution and black for the Defence - we limit the number of documents that will become exhibits, especially yesterday with the maps. I think we all experienced that reducing the number of maps as exhibits would not be bad. So that is a suggestion to the parties not to tender them into evidence. And of course, the other party is always free that if we say we cannot work in whatever way with this map, they always can tender their own maps in evidence. But it would be highly appreciated if the parties could at least compromise on what map is to be used, otherwise, we get really confused. I now come to what happens once a document has become an exhibit. Whenever a document has become an exhibit, the parties are supposed to put the P, for Prosecution, or the D, for Defence, and the numbers on the copies they have been provided with already. But if a document has been marked by a witness, copies of the exhibit, so that's the marked exhibit, will have to be provided to the parties. The Registry will take care of that. If the parties want to have these copies on short notice, this will only be possible if the exhibits will be copied by the Office of the Prosecutor. This would mean that the chain of custody for which the Registry is responsible has to be broken for a short period of time and merely for reproduction. I invite the Defence to agree with such a short break. If the Defence would not agree, of course, it's entirely up to you to make up your mind. If the Defence does not agree, it might cause considerable delays in receiving the copies of the marked documents. I add to that that whether the original that will be given back to the Registrar after having been reproduced by the Office of the Prosecutor, whether any changes as far as the markings are concerned can be seen. It is always possible to verify whether these are still the original markings or whether anything has been changed by watching the trial video in which the marking of the document as such is shown. So this Chamber thinks that there is hardly any risk that any document would be changed while being reproduced by the Office of the Prosecutor. But I leave it up to the Defence on whether they will agree with this procedure. And I indicated how it is possible to verify that no changes are made. The exhibits that finally stay with the Registry are always there for inspection upon request by the parties. This is the order for documents we decided upon, apart from this specific procedure for reproduction in order to speed up the return of the exhibits, the marked exhibits, to the parties. I would like to hear either now or on short notice from the Defence whether they would agree with this short break in the chain of custody for these marked exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has listened carefully to what you have just set out. And with regard to documents listed as exhibit, when it comes to maps, the Defence would like to make a suggestion, if it may. As evidence by the Prosecution, the black and white map of Sarajevo was introduced in the scale of 1 to 12.000, and after that, a map with markings which the witness made in response to questions from the Prosecution, and afterwards, the Defence was allowed to utilize that map, and the Defence will be tendering the map as an exhibit. I should like to suggest that the Prosecution and Defence in future use this same map when witnesses are being examined, and the Defence would like to request that a clear copy of this one map be handed to the Defence as well so as to coordinate our effort and that we use the same map for the examination of witnesses. When examination of the witness is over, the Defence accepts your suggestion that a copy of that map which has been tendered into evidence as an exhibit be copied, and that one copy be placed with the Defence and the other with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you also accept that there will be a short break of the chain of custody. And this, of course, is only valid for the exhibits of the Prosecution because all the exhibits the Defence will tender, if there are any markings on it, they will be reproduced by the Registry. So it's only just -- so the chain of custody will not be broken if it concerns exhibits with a D on it, Defence exhibits. As far as I understand, parties do agree that usually we'll use the map that has been -- the blank map that has been tendered into evidence. You also agree that during examination-in-chief and during cross-examination, they may be marked with different colours, and then finally the party who called the witness tender the map marked as it is into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With the comment that I made, that the map with the markings of positions where the witness indicated certain positions in response to questions from the cross-examination, the Defence will tender into evidence as well. I think we agree on that point. So we'll be using one and the same map all the time, a copy of this one map which the Prosecution and the Defence will have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as Mr. Kovac is concerned, the map will be tendered twice in evidence, once with the red markings and once with the black markings, and for the future they will be tendered only one time in evidence with both colour of markings on it. Thank you very much. I'm quite glad we could agree on that. Then I would invite to the Defence to give a response to the suggestion that has been made by the Prosecution yesterday. I see it was at 10 minutes past 4.00, but I'm not quite sure whether the time is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President. I thank the Chamber for according us this opportunity. The Trial Chamber could have seen through the testimony of the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yesterday to what point it is important to be able to note what the attitudes of witnesses are, especially when this begins by asking you whether -- because he began by asking you whether he was obliged to answer questions put to him by the Defence. This led us to think that it was not right to follow the oral motion formulated by the Prosecution simply because we believe that your Trial Chamber must at all times be able to appreciate the manner in which testimony is given, as well as the contents. So the form and the contents. And taking the example of yesterday's witness, at one point he contradicted himself, and we have a point to make with respect to that. The witness said that what he had said previously during the examination-in-chief was not what he actually meant but was the result of a mistake in the interpretation or translation. I think at this stage, it would be useful for the Chamber to hear the tapes played again, and we can verify to see what the answer was, whether it was really a different answer or an error in interpretation. And as to basics, there will be other testimonies where the Defence and the Trial Chamber would like to see how witnesses comport themselves, in not only what they say, because -- and we have a negative answer to the proposal made by the Prosecution yesterday at around 1600 hours. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I may invite the parties to continue whatever communications as how to speed up the trial without losing any of the rights or any of the aspects that the party thinks of as important for the case. But I can imagine that on some issues, that at least perhaps on a few more issues, that some compromise would be possible. For example, yesterday, we went through a lot of areas of the town again, and the witness was asked a couple of times, what is this area, what's that area? I think if you would compromise on what areas there are and where they are on this map, that would, perhaps, speed up the questioning of the witness. But I leave it to the parties, but I invite them to continue to communicate whatever might be useful to make this trial as efficient as possible. Then -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Might I clarify one of the points that you had set out in relation to the tendering of proposed exhibits, and that is point 2. I think you said, Mr. President, that the party who intends to tender a document should indicate that at the first time that it is put to the witness. But if I could explain my concern by way of example, if a witness was being examined in chief and shown a document, as the directions given by you presently read, as I understand it, that would be the point at which the counsel would indicate to the Trial Chamber that it is their intention to tender that document. But of course, at that point, there may be no proper basis to tender it. That would depend in most cases upon what answers the witness gave in relation to the document. I assume that you have in mind, Mr. President, that the time for making submissions both for and against the tender are after those relevant questions have been asked of the witness, that is, at a point in time that the examining counsel is of the view that the document in this example has been shown to have sufficient probative value in order for it to be tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Of course, that's also the reason why I used the word "intends" to tender. Of course, the development of the examination of the witness may be such that finally, the document loses all its relevance. But one of the reasons why I proposed this is that if the other party, and I expect the parties to communicate to each other prior to the examination of the witness of what documents they intend to use -- I'm not saying to tender into evidence, but what documents they are going to use during the examination of a witness so the other party can see, whether, for example, it's a forgery or not so that they can make the kind of objections that you can make at this moment. And then of course after the examination of the witnesses, we'll see whether there's still probative value, whether it's relevant or not, and so then we come to these kind of issues. But I would try to avoid any situation where a witness is confronted with a document which the other party thinks to be a forgery so that at least there's an opportunity at that moment to comment on that. It's a very practical solution, and I do understand that the intention might change during the examination of the witness. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just wish to indicate to the Chamber that the Defence is in agreement with this but that there are problems, that is to say, to see what the Prosecution -- how these problems can be treated in order to reduce the number of problems and cut down the number of exhibits. Thank you for your attention, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We spend 20 to 25 minutes on the issue. I hope it will save us a lot of time in the future. It's now, Ms. Pilipovic, you have the -- you may proceed now, after the witness Kovac has been brought in, with the cross-examination of Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one point, I'm sorry. The Defence needs to finalize a document, and the Defence would like to know when we will have the break because depending on that, and in order to respect the time limit, I may need to be absent, and I would prefer to do so before the witness is heard, if that will not disturb the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to continue, as a matter of fact, and I think the break will be as usual at a quarter to 4.00, since Ms. Pilipovic indicated yesterday that she would need one more hour. That would be approximately at the end of the cross-examination of the witness, and perhaps you can then do whatever you need to do during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me and can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I may remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you made the day before yesterday. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the cross-examination yesterday, we stopped when you were discussing Rajlovac. So could I ask the usher for his assistance to show the witness the map that we were using yesterday. Can we proceed, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you showed us where Rajlovac is. Could you now make a circle around it and mark it with a letter "R."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Brijesce Brdo and Grbavica were under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who had control over Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajlovac was under the control of the forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw the separation line between the two warring parties in this area, between Rajlovac and Sokolje --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't do that because I wasn't familiar with that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We haven't established that he has any knowledge of this particular line that is being questioned about. With respect, I think my learned friend should establish that the witness has any foundation of knowledge upon which to then perform the act which she is asked to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you like to answer on the first of the two issues raised by the Prosecution. The first is that you indicated no time during which the separation line could be there, while questioning. The second one is that the witness has indicated several times that he has no knowledge of the exact situation of separation lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the objection of my learned friends opposite. The witness has marked Rajlovac upon my request. If I have to indicate the time, I am referring to every time I put a question to the witness, I can repeat that I am referring to the period 1992, 1993, 1994. That is while the conflict in Sarajevo was ongoing. The witness, in answer to my question, said he didn't know, and I said thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: With respect, I have to raise one further thing. My learned friend has made reference to 1992 in its entirety. I think she should specify precisely when in 1992. It has already been indicated in evidence that lines did change, so we must have a more precise indication of time if any particular thing is going to be marked on a map as being the extant position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are talking about the relevant period for which General Galic stands accused, that is, from September 1992 to August 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that clear enough for the Prosecution, September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There are only the two observations I would make on that, Your Honours. Firstly, that if the witness is to be asked to place something permanently on a map, we should know clearly whether that was a permanent situation throughout the period. The period we now understand on record is September 1992 to August 1994. However, there may have been changes, and it should be made clear, I think, with respect to my learned friend's questioning as to precisely what point, if there are any areas where such features changed. The second one I would submit goes back to the one I mentioned already, there should be foundational questions to establish whether or not the witness in question has adequate knowledge to be requested to mark a map with something which will then go on record as if he had spoken it. And clearly, simply a line on a map does not show whether it has been qualified by an absence or a presence of true knowledge for making that mark. Those are my only observations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. As far as your first remark is concerned, I would say that the witness has testified that he can't draw the line, it's useless at this moment to discuss any further what period of time this line would cover. But perhaps for the future, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Pilipovic, the Prosecution would like to have it as precise as possible in order to avoid any misunderstanding. As far as the second issue is concerned, may I suggest to you -- let me first clarify the suggestion I will make to you. I don't know what you want to establish, whether the precise position of the separation lines, if that is your intention, then perhaps a general answer just a suggestion could be whether the witness has any specific knowledge on the separation line and perhaps where he has knowledge -- to what extent he has knowledge of that. If it is your intention to establish whether the witness has any knowledge of separation lines, perhaps this could also be asked to the witness in a more general way. These are just suggestions in order to -- in order to lose no time on issues that can be clarified quicker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will respond to the issues raised by my learned friend. Regarding the positions, the question was as to whether the lines had changed. The position of my learned friends is that the lines were static throughout the conflict. Secondly, in answer to my question whether he had been interviewed by the investigators on the 3rd of October, 2000, the witness said he had. I showed him yesterday a part of his statement when he said that the Civil Defence was informed through the defence ministry about the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This statement by the witness prompted the Defence to put such questions to the witness as he, himself, said that through the Civil Defence, he had information about positions. Now, to what extent and in what area he was informed about, he will tell us. In answer to my latest question, he said that in this area, he was not informed. He had no knowledge. Also, by putting these questions to the witness, the Defence would like, in view of the position the witness had throughout the duration of the conflict, to check the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the witness, if he could, to look in the south-westerly direction on the map, and to mark for us what part of town that is, what is the name of this district of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't orientate myself. What part of you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: South-West in relation to Rajlovac. Go down the map. Tell us if not.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this area here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Further down. Or let me put it this way, do you know where Ilidza is, the district of Ilidza? Yes, of course. If you can, will you please mark it and put the letter "I."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether during the conflict, from September 1992 until August 1994, who controlled Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilidza was under the control of the forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to when the conflict broke out in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably at the beginning of 1992. I think it was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the parties in conflict were?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army and the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you -- would you agree with me that throughout the duration of the conflict in Sarajevo, separation lines existed, had been established?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, when were those lines established?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the middle of 1992, in my opinion, according to information I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the middle of the year, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean May, June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a part of Sarajevo was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what part you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have just marked for us the parts of Sarajevo that were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of Sarajevo was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within Sarajevo, the municipalities of Centar, Stari Grad, Novi Grad, that there were separation lines there, too?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Separation lines remained in the territory of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Sarajevo was a divided city?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a smaller extent, it was divided.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that between these two armies, as we have been referring to them, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska, that there was constant fighting on a daily basis along the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that there was fighting on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with respect to the map, the witness -- the Defence has no further questions, and we would like to suggest that the maps, together with the markings made by Mr. Kovac, be tendered into evidence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, this map, this marked map with the black marks on it, is admitted into evidence. And it will bear what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you tell us in your opinion when the conflict started in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "conflict."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge as to when the conflict at the police school in Vrace occurred?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that conflict, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which month it was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that it was in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when an immediate threat of war was proclaimed by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of May, or rather the end of April, 1992. I think that is when it was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory. Was it on the 5th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it wasn't on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you told us that you do have knowledge about the conflict at the police school in Vrace, do you know that that was when the police force was divided on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened on the 1st of March, 1992 at Bas Carsija?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In March and April 1992 and somewhat later, do you know that the population was moving out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March and April?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And May.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In May, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When in May did the population start to move out of Sarajevo? When in May, the first half of May or the second half of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I think it was the first half of May when the operations started. That is when the war started in terms of its intensity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please ask again your question which appears on page 17, line 24, because interpreter couldn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the Vrace police school, there was a conflict, and that the police force was divided on ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, I learned about it from the media. That's what I said. I learned about it through the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn from the media that on the 1st of March, 1992, a civilian was killed at Bas Carsija who was in a wedding group, and do you know that he was killed by Ramiz Dalalic as was reported by the media?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that event and I learned about it from the media again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were barricades put up then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the conflict broke out in May. Between whom in May did the conflict break out?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed officially? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific knowledge about it, but I can say that it was sometime at the end of April 1992. I just know that before that, there was the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the Territorial Defence, which other units joined to form the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units of the HVO, I think, some units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You talked to us yesterday about units that had their leaders such as Juka Prazina, Musan Topalovic. Do you know that those units also became part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they did, but I have no specific knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military police also became part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you lived at Alipasino Polje, do you know that the commander of the military police at Dobrinja was Kerim Loncarevic, known as "Doctor"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had learned about Kerim Loncarevic as commander, but I learned through the media. But I didn't know where he was located nor which unit he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that from the media?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did the planning for the activities of the Civil Defence -- when was it made in view of the situation that was in force?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plans for the activities of the Civil Defence were made on the basis of an assessment of the situation, that is, an assessment of the situation that existed with respect to the situation and the conditions of life of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the Civil Defence staff, the one you were in, was there a commander of the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was his rank? Was he commander of the Civil Defence of Sarajevo or did you have commanders by municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were staffs by municipalities, that is, commanders at the level of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that through your commissioners, you distributed humanitarian aid to the population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we informed them about humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who made out the lists?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean of the population?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the persons, the civilians that were going to receive humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lists were made by Civil Defence commissioners by buildings and neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time you held that position, and I'm referring to the period from April 1992 until the end of the conflict in Sarajevo, were you wearing a uniform, the kind you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you start wearing it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wore it at the beginning of the war, and then for a while I wore civilian clothes because the uniform had got worn out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about other members of Civil Defence? Did they also wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they wore the uniforms left over from the former Civil Defence, if I can put it that way, the Civil Defence that was operational before the war. These were uniforms that people held at home. In fact, they were blue overalls with the symbol of the Civil Defence on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they suits or overalls?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were suits, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina wear such uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While performing your duties as head of the Civil Defence staff for Novi Grad, did you have any discussions with the civilians, with the population? Did they come to see you asking for assistance, to complain about shortages of water, electricity and so on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such conversations, but we would also frequently tour the local communities. And through our commissioners, we would be briefed on problems locally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Through your commissioners, did you personally have information from the inhabitants to the effect that their family members were being arrested and taken in an unknown direction?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the distribution of humanitarian aid was conducted at certain localities, and that those spots or points were changed from time to time. Do you happen to know that humanitarian aid was distributed to civilians at the separation line?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that kind. That would have been too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at Dobrinja and Alipasino Polje, and more specifically, on the square which was the Zavnobih square, whether there were apartment buildings acting as prisons where Serbs were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at Alipasino Polje, on that particular square, there was a cafe called the Borsalino cafe?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, yes, the Borsalino coffee bar did exist in Alipasino Polje settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the cafe working during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know with respect to your municipality how many in percentages were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, the percentages for the population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, during the war, and after the war, if you can tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war -- I'm giving you rough figures. I can't give you the exact figures. I don't have them. But roughly speaking, before the war, there were approximately 65 percent Bosniaks, 25 percent Serbs, and approximately 8 to 10 percent were Croats and others. A small negligible percentage of miscellaneous. That would be my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How about after the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, that figure was reduced. When I say reduced, I mean that the number of Bosniaks increased, in fact, whereas the number of Serbs decreased, and the number of Croats decreased somewhat as well. I think that today in the Novi Grad municipality, there are approximately 15 percent Serbs and approximately 5 to 6 percent Croats, and the rest would be various, depending on how they declared themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Civil Defence staffs, did they have units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which units were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Civil Defence units of a general purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they specialised units?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the local communities, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And at the level of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a special unit for protection against fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And the specialised unit against fire, what was the national composition of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were approximately 70 percent Bosniaks, approximately 25 percent were Serbs, and 5 percent were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How did you come by those figures, on the basis of what data?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my free assessment on the basis of the people I knew, although we would never strictly divide people up according to their ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that Sarajevo had the problem of sniping.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were sniper incidents reported to you personally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that doesn't come under our competencies and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to know that on the high-rise buildings in the old part of town and in the centre of town of the city of Sarajevo, like the Energoinvest building, the executive council building, the Momo & Uzeir building, and the electricity board building, that there were sniper nests at the top of these buildings and that they were snipers belonging to the Muslim army? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about the problem of shelling in Sarajevo yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I correct something with respect to the Muslim army that you asked a moment ago? It was not the Muslim army. It was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because when you say "Muslim," then that determines the composition of that army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed that in my questions, I usually referred to it as the BH army. Could you tell me something about the problem of shelling? When did the shelling occur in the course of the day or night, give us a time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it's difficult to say when and determine the time. Sometime the shellings would start early on at dawn, at daybreak, and would go on until 12.00 noon. There would be a lull until 3.00 or 4.00, and then the shelling would continue and would go on until 10.00 p.m. or maybe 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to distinguish between the intensity of the shelling during the day and its intensity at night?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to note any difference. If the shelling started at night, then it would go on until the early morning hours. And quite certainly, according to physical laws, sounds are much stronger -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the sounds of shelling is much stronger during the night, much louder. So that the shelling in the course of the night caused greater unrest and fear in town, although the people were in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that there was frequent shelling, and you said that it would be usually early in the morning and go on the whole day, or that it would begin in early evening and go on throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were periods like that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you hear shelling in the course of the night, could you tell who was doing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could hear the shots being fired because at night, especially after midnight, it was generally quiet. That is a natural law, I suppose, that it's quieter at night. And then you could hear the shooting coming from the surrounding hills first, which broke this silence, especially from Trebevic. And after that, judging by the sounds of the shells, you could tell which settlement was being targeted or where the targeting -- the shooting was coming from. If you were at the positions at Alipasino Polje, for example, when the shelling was going on, you could hear very well the shooting of -- shells being shot from guns and artillery pieces from the Trebevic locality. Three to four seconds later, you could hear the whiz-whiz of a shell, which would then explode somewhere nearby. It would have its destructive power several instances later. May I just add, what is important here to note is that the calibres were stronger, large calibres, and they were -- they reverberated in the settlement. When the shell hit an object, the high-rise buildings and apartment buildings would tremble and shake, and the people who were living in those buildings at the time were never sure that they would survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the geographic position of Sarajevo, and you said the surrounding hills, does Sarajevo's geographic position allow you to determine what direction the shell is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From certain locations, yes, because some artillery weapons were placed above the town itself on the hills surrounding the city, whereas the artillery pieces that were used for indirect targeting were behind the hills surrounding the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You were very precise and specific in answering that question. Where do you get that knowledge from, from the media, or did you visit those positions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is knowledge I obtained from people who were professionals in that field. And if you call them as witnesses, I'm sure they will be able to tell this august Trial Chamber about what happened in much greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally hear the sound of a shell or just the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, during -- from 1992 to 1994, I heard the whizzing by of shells, and it is a very specific sound that instills fear. It is a very frightening sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received humanitarian aid through humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which humanitarian organisations did you cooperate with on the territory of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a system by which humanitarian aid was brought in and it went via the municipal staff and was dispatched to the staffs of the Civil Defence organisation in the local communities. Because at the level of the municipal staff and headquarters, we organised the vehicles for transporting the aid and the people to do it, and people directly drove the humanitarian aid to the different local communities and distributed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On your own municipality, were there organisations which produced food or clothing, manufactured clothing, to supply the civilian population with?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the sewing workshops that we set up to help the population, the tailoring establishments to supply the population with clothes. And we received food exclusively through the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the tailoring workshops that were set up sewed clothing. Did they also sew uniforms for the soldiers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As you cooperated with the headquarters of the BH army, could you tell us where those headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what area you have in mind. For what area and what level of organisation do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean at the level of the brigades and at the level of corps, and the main staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We maintained contacts through the municipal staff and headquarters, and then at the level of the president of the municipality, if it was necessary to meet and discuss matters of general importance for the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the main body that you coordinated with which was in charge of the defence of the town, that you had meetings with?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the defence of the town was concerned, the military body, the main military body, and that was the 1st Corps, the 1st Corps of the BH army. As far as our relationship with the corps was concerned, it went via the municipal staff for Civil Defence and its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was the general mobilisation proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, it was sometime at the end of April and beginning of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the municipalities and the town, were crisis staffs or war staffs set up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking about staffs? No, there were [Realtime transcript read in error "presidents"] presidencies. I remember that presidencies existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As you said that you had contact with the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the highest military body and authority in Sarajevo, what about your municipality, what centre did you have contacts with?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't contact any military centre because no military existed for the municipality level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I interrupt for a second. I think there is a mistranscript at line 8 of this page 29. I think the response of the witness is "presidencies," as opposed to "presidents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noted that as well. I thought it would be corrected overnight. I think Ms. Pilipovic will also agree that it was "presidencies" instead of "presidents."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know which --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do it again. There is a gap as well, I see, line 7 of the transcript of this page, there is an answer given which was a question, and then there is a "Q" followed by a blank. It comes just before the answer, "No, there were presidents." So we have a problem there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, the witness continued his answering, although Ms. Pilipovic tried to formulate her next question. But if necessary, I think we could hear the audiotape later on. I don't think it will create great misunderstandings if we continue. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you happen to know what artillery pieces the corps of the BH army had?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict from September 1992 and in 1993, did you happen to see or notice a tank that was in the tunnel at the Ciglana settlement?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How in your municipality did you regulate the question of repairs for the water supply system and power supply system?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were services from the water supply service and the power supply service, and they were in charge of each municipality. Actually, there were professional men who, in cooperation with the local Civil Defence units, dealt with any breakdowns in the system. And the members of the Civil Defence would help them physically in putting the matter right, whereas these professionals would actually undertake the repair work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the transformer stations which supplied your municipality with electricity? Where were they located? In what part of town?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of transformer stations. Every settlement had its own transformer station, and in one settlement, there would even be several transformer stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And you were successful in dealing with the breakdowns of the system?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we cooperated with professional teams. And when there was electricity -- because there were frequent power cuts, and for some periods, the town would be left without any electricity at all for longer periods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about gas? Did you have gas?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was until the beginning of the winter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, there was no more gas?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would come and go. Mostly we didn't have any gas. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would say that there was an absence of gas, rather than not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As the head of Civil Defence, do you happen to know that the population of Sarajevo were not able to leave the town without a permit authorizing them to do so?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know about that. That was probably under the competence of some other service or organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that such services existed, or rather, how could people leave town? What did they need if they wanted to leave town?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As you are the head of the Civil Defence staff for the Sarajevo canton at present, could you tell us: In the canton of Sarajevo, if you happen to have the information, how many Serbs are there, how many Muslims or Bosniaks, and how many Croats, if you can answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I should like to clarify the situation for the Trial Chamber. I think that during the war, especially at the beginning of the war, there was an exodus of Serbs from Sarajevo. But I have to state that a large number of people of Serb ethnicity also stayed on in Sarajevo. Many left, but many stayed. Those who left, left, I think, for a number of reasons. Some were asked to leave and to join those who did not agree with the then policy and politics. Others left from fear; they were afraid of the war. And others stayed on, together with the other ethnic groups and people to bear the burden of war. All of us together esteem very highly of those people who stayed on. To answer your question, I have to explain to the Trial Chamber how the situation was in general, which had an effect and determined the number of Serbs who stayed, the present figures. So on the basis of these facts and figures, in order to answer the question I have just been asked and to give it legal strength in the determination of certain facts, the essential thing is to see the reason for the Serbs leaving Sarajevo during the war, why they left. I remember a programme at the beginning of the war where the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was a very simple one. All I asked him was whether the witness knows how many Serbs are now living in Sarajevo, and Bosniaks, Muslims, Croats. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, the question was rather limited, and you give a lot of explanation, perhaps, on what finally will be your answer. But perhaps if you would restrict yourself to first answering the question. If a further explanation is asked, I'm quite sure that counsel will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at present in the city, if you're thinking of the situation at present, a large number -- well, not a large number, but a substantial number of Serbs are coming back to the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us how many, if you know. If you do not, say you do not know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the percentage now is between 20 and 25 percent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And one more question: What was -- what purpose did the tunnel serve? What was its function in Sarajevo? And do you know who dug the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to answer your question, I have to explain some facts to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, I'd just like to know from Ms. Pilipovic how much more time she would need for cross-examination, or was is this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question. I would just like the witness to answer and to tell me when the tunnel was made and whether he knows who took part in digging the tunnel. That's all. So just a very short question, whether he knows it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, would you please answer this question. And whether there are any other questions, we will see then.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the tunnel was dug sometime at the end of the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who did the digging?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units whose work obligation it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the national composition of the units doing this work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic affiliation was not a question that was considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before having a break, would the Prosecution -- is the Prosecution in need of further re-examination, not to start it right away, but just in order to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is just one small area we would like to address, and I'm sure we will be most brief in so doing. I have about two or three questions all of which require only a short answer. After the break, if you prefer, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I prefer to do it after the break. We will have a break now, if you could please guide the witness out of the courtroom, and bring Mr. Galic out of the courtroom. We'll have a break until 4.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you concluded the cross-examination of Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence would have one more question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say one more, I'll allow that. You may proceed once the witness has been --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness. Mr. Kovac, the Defence has asked to put one more question to you, which was allowed to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you told us that the tunnel was dug in 1993. Would you just tell us, please, the position of the tunnel and who organised the able-bodied persons who were under work obligation, as you said, to dig that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who organised it. It was probably at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which level?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably of the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the military or members of the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of digging that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that when the tunnel was dug through, there was more food because there was a shortage of food in town. We received humanitarian aid that was limited in quantity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That was the question that I asked to put to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. The Prosecution now has an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions that actually go back to the days of your training as a military policeman in compulsory service. I believe you said to my learned friend that there were different types of policemen in time of peace and in time of war. Can you tell us what the differences in the duties were in times of peace or in times of war for military policemen?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about regular military service and how I was trained in the unit as a military policeman, there were peacetime and wartime duties. The peacetime duties were daily duties which were carried out also by the civilian police but it related only to military personnel, that is, to members of the army, ordinary soldiers and officers. If we're talking about wartime duties, the military police was trained to carry out special tasks which could not be carried out by regular soldiers. Their duties were to engage in some smaller scale but specific wartime assignments. It's something like attempts to break into the territory under the control of that army as a group, the elimination of certain military targets, which were specific to that military unit. Those would roughly be the differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I believe you agreed, I think, with my learned friend when she put the question that the peacetime duties certainly of military police included patrolling and arresting military personnel for discipline and other matters, criminal matters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, in accordance with your training, who would give the orders to military police officers to perform an arrest?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Who would those superiors be? Would they be within the military police or would they be other superiors within the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the command, whether it was under the brigade or a larger military unit that the military police was in. Within the framework of those military formations, there were security departments, and those orders would be issued by the officers in command of those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. departments. In my view, those would be, as far as I understood, on the basis of my military service, were the heads of security who were part of the command. They were members of the command of a particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So when a police or a military officer performed an arrest, to whom was that military police officer ordered to hand over the person that he had arrested?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is based on my experience from my military service days, serving in the former Yugoslav people's army. For instance, it depended on the case. Persons were taken into custody to the unit and escorted to units of the former Yugoslav people's army from which they came. For instance, if they had fled from the unit - we had such cases - or if they had committed any criminal offence, then there were military prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Now, taking account you've described additional wartime duties, did the military police still perform those discipline, patrolling, and arrest duties in time of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Or in accordance with your training, in a time of war, would military police officers still perform the same duties as they performed in peacetime and then have additional duties that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duty is to assist, or rather to keep the situation in check in wartime, probably together with all others, to prevent any disorder or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And would, therefore, military police have the same powers of arrest in accordance with your training, the same powers of arrest in wartime as they would have had in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. Probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That actually concludes my re-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. One of the Judges will put questions to the witness, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, at the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned different types of bullets. We all know that the use of certain types of bullets is forbidden by international law. My question is, do you know whether those forbidden bullets were used by the parties during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to say. I don't know. Possibly they were, but I don't know because I had no personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Have you heard about, for example, dumdum bullets?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Did you use dumdum bullets when you were in your compulsory service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't use them, but our superiors in the former Yugoslav People's Army told us about those types of weapons. We studied about them in books, but we didn't use them, nor did -- nor were such bullets used during exercises or target shooting when they were organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Elmahdi, do you have any additional questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, I'm aware of the great burden that you have suffered during the past two days, but I would like, if you could, obtain some information from you regarding three points: The first has to do with the media to which you referred on a number of occasions. You said, "Yes, I learned such and such a thing through the media." Which media were you referring to? Were they the media -- the national media, international media? Could you clarify that point a little for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the media, there were regular programmes on the radio and television when there was electricity. So the TV could be watched when there was electricity, and the radio when the electricity was cut. So these were the regular daily information programmes which, in addition to local news, also carried news reports from CNN and other international broadcasters. Those were the state-controlled media, which, in my view, were up to the standards required for an objective and timely information of the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovac. Another question, if you don't mind: You said, and I quote -- I will do it in English. [In English] "The Land Registry Department took with them part of the documentation and the maps from Sarajevo, and probably it was those maps that they used to be able to ascertain with great precision where these locations were." [Interpretation] My question is the following: For you, this taking of documents and maps, is it something you are sure of based on concrete knowledge, or is it simply your conclusion? Is it a personal opinion that you have? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion regarding documents which depicted the infrastructural position of various facilities in the municipalities was based on the statements made by people who used to work in the Land Registry Departments of the municipalities within the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard people talking about certain documents being taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my last question, if you don't mind, you also said - and I quote in English again - [In English]: "Some of the inhabitants of the Novi Grad municipality had left following certain directives." [Interpretation] Who gave those directions and who left?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is to primarily the departure of the Serb population from the city. And this quotation is based on the fact that at the beginning of the war, the leadership, the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs had called on the Sarajevan Serbs to come out of the city saying that Sarajevo was not their homeland, and that they would be better off in their native towns and places outside Sarajevo, that they would be more comfortable. This was published in the media, and I think this was at the beginning of the war in the prime-time newscast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I've just two small questions for you. You have been talking about a tunnel, not being able to say exactly where it was. Could you say perhaps in more general terms, the tunnel was connecting what to what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one views the position of the tunnel in logical terms, and it went from the neighbourhood of Dobrinja, or rather, C5, towards the neighbourhood of Butmir, so it would be logical to assume that people who were making these assessments as to where a necessary entry and exit point for the city should be made, came to the conclusion that that would be the most suitable location, and the tunnel went beneath the Sarajevo airport. That is where the separation lines probably were more considerable, so that this area, from the security standpoint regarding the movement of people through that tunnel, was safer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You already answered my second question: underneath what the tunnel was. If there are no more questions from my colleagues, I would like to thank you, Mr. Kovac, from coming from so far in order to answer the questions of the parties and of this Chamber. Thank you very much for coming. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, who is the next witness you're calling?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I'll ask the usher to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Mandilovic, do you hear me in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you, Mr. President, yes. THE COURT: Mr. Mandilovic, Rule 90(a) requires you, being called as a witness by the Prosecution, to give a solemn declaration in which the text will be handed over to you. And may I invite you to make this solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandilovic. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, it will be I, again, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed in your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, would you be so kind as to give your full name to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you say, please, where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of June, 1949 in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me where Novi Sad is, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Serbia, the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us very briefly in what profession you are qualified. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a doctor, physician, a general practitioner, and a specialist for ear, nose, and throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where do you currently practise, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I currently practise in the state hospital or rather, today, it is called the general hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you moved from Serbia to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When I was four years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After you had qualified in the medical profession, in what context did you practice your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When I graduated from the faculty of medicine, I did my compulsory medical training in Sarajevo. And after that, I did my military service as a doctor serving in the military hospital in Meljine, which is in the former socialist republic of Montenegro. After that, upon completing my military service, I responded to a competition for posts inside the Yugoslav people's army, and I got the post as general in the Sarajevo Garrison, or rather the Sarajevo Garrison infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you say when it was that you started to take up your duties then in the Sarajevo Garrison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In August 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the JNA have a military hospital in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was there a presence of a JNA military hospital right the way up to the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
