utterances.text: And Doctor, we have already heard in this Chamber that in about May 1992, the war started in Sarajevo. What is your -- very briefly, your recollection of what was happening in Sarajevo at that time, at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: The situation was difficult in the city of Sarajevo but the difficult situation began earlier on, right at the start of the year 1992. The situation was unstable. There was tension, and there was an era of expectation and uncertainty and insecurity. And that was the situation as of January. It went through February and March, and all this escalated slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there a time that it became an open conflict of some description?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Individual conflicts were frequent, particularly in the month of April. But I think as far as I see it, and as far as I remember, they were individual conflicts, and later on, there was a real escalation sometime on the 6th of April, around about the 6th of April. And then tensions grew, the situation came to a head. And in May, there was a substantially different situation, one which spoke absolutely of -- was -- a situation of war was manifest, became absolutely manifest at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you say a situation of war became manifest, could you tell me whether that had anything to do with any shelling, artillery shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It did. But artillery shelling of the city during that period of time was far smaller than it was to be later on. I apologise. We're talking about April and the start of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I've moved into the month of May 1992. Did this shelling situation persist up to the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And it escalated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And at the time in May, what was the status of the JNA hospital you were working in? Was it still a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The military hospital had the kind of status that it did up until the 12th or the 14th of May. I can't quite remember from the passage of time what the exact dates were. But the Yugoslav People's Army or the cadres of the Yugoslav people's army, to be more exact, according to their own volition left the hospital. From that time on, the military hospital changed its title, and it became the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did it fall under any kind of alternative military control, or did it fall under civilian administration when it changed its status?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It fell under civilian administration. The management of the hospital was made up of civilians, doctors who had worked in the hospital prior to that and who had stayed on in the hospital, remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in fact, is that what you did, Doctor, stay on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I wasn't a member of the management.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, if I may, could I take you forward to September of 1992 and the winter that went from 1992 to 1993. Now, at that time, what was the situation as regards shelling or any other kind of shooting and any effects it may have had on or around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As time passed, so the situation in town became more complicated in the negative sense. The shelling of the town became more frequent and sniping started as well. And as a direct consequence of that, we saw successively an increasing number of casualties, both from the sniping and from the mortar projectiles and their dispersive effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to ask you more about that later. In the meantime, can you tell us whether in 1992 - this is from September onwards - the hospital buildings themselves suffered any damage from these activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The hospital building itself was on several occasions directly hit with certain types of projectiles, so that the facade of the hospital, the windows - the glass of the windows - all that was damaged and destroyed, shattered. And that could be seen from the photographs taken of that period. All the hospital floors - and there were 12 of them - were devastated in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you speak to the facade of the hospital, in which direction did that facade face? Can you say what areas were in front of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The broader facade of the hospital faced north and south. The narrower sides faced west and east. The southern side, the southern facade of the hospital, was mostly damaged, although damage did exist on the eastern and western facades as well. Later on, after 1992, the facade on the northerly side was also damaged but to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in towards which areas did the southern side of the hospital face? Can you give us the names of any of the areas facing you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The south side of the hospital in general terms faces the reaches of the mountain or rather hill of Trebevic, which is in the immediate vicinity of the town. And we can also mention opposite the hospital is the Jewish cemetery, and a little more westerly, there's another settlement and a small elevation which was called Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which district, in which district the Jewish cemetery is located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The Jewish cemetery is located at the same altitude as the hospital across the Mijecka River at the start of the slopes of Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And those areas you're referring to opposite the hospital, who actually held at that time, at the end of 1992, who or what forces held the area of the Jewish cemetery and the parts of Trebevic you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: They were the forces of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And about how far in a direct line from the hospital were the -- let us say the confrontation or separation lines, do you recall at that time, the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that they were about 300 to 400 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I believe you said that is on the south side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The south side, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any other confrontation lines in the -- well, close to the hospital, say, on the east, the west, or the north?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course there were. Yes, because the city of Sarajevo is not a large city in terms of space, and these were mostly in the old part of town, the centre of town, and parts closer to the old part of town so that, in practical terms, towards the east is the end of town, which is encircled by mountains. And so quite certainly, towards the east of the hospital, there were military conflicts going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were any other areas of military conflict quite as close to the hospital as the one you've referred to where the Jewish cemetery was 300 to 400 metres away?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you restate -- rephrase your question? I'm not sure I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let me put another way. You've referred to the lines on the south side of the hospital as 300 to 400 metres. Were any other confrontation lines as close to the hospital as those ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make, Mr. President, for the same reasons that were expounded a moment ago by my learned friend. One must be certain of the time and period. If we're asking questions, we must limit the question in terms of time, what period of time is my learned friend referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when I look at line 15 of page 47, it indicates to me that the questioning is about the end of 1992. You mean that we need any further specification or... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is that we have a succession of questions, a chain of questions, so I would like to know whether we're still talking about the same period. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please verify whether we are still in the same time era.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm talking exclusively at this time of the period September 1992 through to the spring of 1993. And all questions at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. point in time, Your Honours, are related to that period and that period alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Having said that, there is just one question on a personal basis I will ask you. As you had stayed in the city up to September 1992, Dr. Mandilovic, had you ever felt at any time that you were free to leave the city if you had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I could leave the city as and when I wanted to. I didn't want to leave, but even if I had, I don't think I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And could you give an indication as to why you feel that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was because you couldn't leave town in any safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mandilovic, we are talking of the winter 1992/1993. Can you tell us what the conditions were as a practising surgeon in that hospital to go about your profession? What was the position regarding your supplies and your working conditions at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the situation in the hospital was difficult, and we can divide it up into two -- the question can be divided up into two sectors, two parts. First, there was no energy, electricity, and the other requirements for the functioning of the hospital. I'm thinking of fuel, electricity, and water. So that is a vital aspect for the normal functioning of a hospital. Without electricity, you cannot have your state of the art machines used. You have a generator, but without fuel to set it into operation, the generator will not work either. Water is a separate issue, and we know how important water is for hygiene. So three vital elements were very much reduced. That is one side of the question. The other side is the medical instruments and medicines. Complex injuries on a daily basis had to be taken care of, and they required post-operative treatment with the use of medicines. It is quite certain that when you are lacking in sufficient supplies and the proper medicines, that treatment will be far more difficult, or rather the chances of treating the patients successfully are lower. And as far as equipment is concerned, equipment is something that is used daily and it has to be repaired and renewed on a regular basis, and we were not able to do that under the prevailing conditions. So that in the process of diagnostics, you were handicapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President, and I apologise for rising to my feet again. The witness still has not answered the penultimate question posed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What question do you exactly mean, then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the one asked by Mr. Blaxill which was formulated, I think it was the penultimate one. It was the one, at any rate, on line -- that is, page 48, between the top and bottom of page 48, Mr. President, or to be more specific, it was lines 9 and 10 of page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: I noticed that, but is it up to the Prosecutor to get the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree. If a witness doesn't answer a question, then, of course the Defence is in a position while cross-examining to come back to that same question and see whether it can get an answer if the Defence thinks they need an answer to that question. Although in general terms, I would say that usually witnesses are answering questions of those who examine them. You may proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At some appropriate time I may just address that issue in a proper context and clarify if it's causing concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you. You were talking of your equipment and all the things that were causing problems for you diagnostically. Now, sir, as a practising surgeon having to undertake surgical procedures, what were the immediate difficulties that you faced in carrying out operations in the theatre? And indeed, were you able to use the theatre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The theatres for surgical interventions were used as rationally as possible. Now, what does that mean? It means that we would switch off the generators and the whole hospital would be in darkness. And when the patient arrived, or a number of patients arrived or a mass of wounded and injured persons, they would be switched on again. And then we had the basic electricity that we needed to perform our surgical interventions. After that, once we had completed surgery, we would switch off the generators so that, throughout that time, we had maximum rationalisation and maximum savings of energy. On the other hand, this also applied to the medicines. We had a maximum reduction and maximum rationalisation. The hospital still had medicines after the departure of the cadres of the Yugoslav people's army. However, those medicines in the course of time became used up slowly so that the hospital was forced or destined, fated to, survive only on the basis of humanitarian aid. Of course, humanitarian aid was never sufficient and can never be satisfactory in quality. In principle, it only caters to minimum standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, aside from those specific difficulties, did the shelling of the hospital or the damage to the hospital cause you to make any arrangements for performing surgery or for the care of your patients within the building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The hospital, as I said at the beginning, has 12 floors, and all the floors are used for the patients, or rather the fourth floor is the surgical theatre. The third floor, sterilization department, and some midwives' premises, and so all the patients in the south wing had to be transferred to the north wing for security reasons. And during certain periods of heavy shelling, all the patients regardless would be taken right down to the ground floor, the cloakrooms of the personnel which we had vacated, cleaned, put hospital beds and equipment there and in that way prepared, improvised hospital rooms with 10, 15, or 20 patients being accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And after the winter of 1992 throughout the year of 1993, were there any changes in the working conditions in the hospital both in terms of your supply and equipment and the safety issues of where you were in the building and where you were able to work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No. The end of 1992 and the whole of 1993 were hard times. The situation didn't change significantly so that the regime or treatment of the patients and our work remained virtually unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Which, in this particular context we're talking about, sir, would bring me to the winter of 1993 and into the spring of 1994. What were your conditions for treating patients during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As we moved forward, I think that the year 1994 brought some light. That is my opinion. I think -- it was such a long time ago, but I think that the situation improved in the logistical sense with the opening of the so-called blue roads, blue routes, when via the airport was used as a road, the airport runways, and when humanitarian aid, medicines, equipment, and food were able to enter the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But prior to that, Doctor, presumably, you had to work through the winter months, from late 1993 into early 1994, and what had your conditions been at that time prior to the blue routes and better supply?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Very hard. I understand the question. Very hard. Today, looking back, it is hard to imagine that you would go without heating in the middle of winter in hospital rooms, in the surgical theatre. So we were all working in a temperature almost the same as the temperature outside. Also, the situation was not improving regarding other sources of energy or medicines, so that was really a very, very difficult period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to turn now and ask you that during these very difficult times, could you tell us, please, that - again, if I can go back if I may to the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993 - can you tell us how much patients, if you can say so on a daily average, how many patients were admitted to the hospital on a daily basis at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: You see, if I may make a point of clarification, to be more precise with my answer, the hospital, as a public institution, worked throughout the war. It had to admit all types of patients, patients who were ill, patients who were injured, and patients injured as a result of war. So one could divide the patients into three categories: Regular patients coming in because of chronic diseases or development of those diseases, injuries that had nothing to do with the war and injuries inflicted by the war. It is hard to say in your medical terms today, but in any event numbers were high. There is no doubt that every day through the hospital clinics and departments, because the hospital consists of various specialist departments, that those -- all the specialist departments certainly tended to more than a hundred patients every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you say you took in patients of all types, and you gave us some categories. Firstly, I would ask, did your patients come from both the civilian and the military sector, i.e. wounded soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give me the portion between let us say those civilians you have referred to here as the war-injured people, and the number of military who would have been treated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, if we are not counting patients who came to the hospital to seek assistance but without suffering from any war injuries, then the ratio between civilians and the military, in my estimate, was about 80 to 20. Maybe -- maybe even a higher percentage in favour of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of those civilians, what would be the type of wounds or injuries that would be treated? And can you give an indication of what the source of those injuries would have been or what inflicted them? I'm sorry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Those injuries were exclusively the consequence of wounding by various kinds of projectiles. The prevalent injuries were those provoked by mortar shells. But there were also injuries caused by classical munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's an expression I don't understand. "Classical munitions," Doctor, could you please give us a definition of what that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert either, but what I meant -- I don't know how to express myself. I meant people hit by bullets, rounds, or small-arms fire, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there some -- I would ask you yourself, did you find yourself performing surgery on wounded people on a daily basis while you were working through the periods we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I could say on a daily basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give us any idea what you would consider or you recall as your general daily workload as a surgeon performing surgical operations day by day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better to put it this way: The shelling of the city were not always of the same intensity. There were days when the shelling was heavier and when it was lighter. And also during the day, there were periods that -- with heavier shelling and with lighter shelling so that it is very difficult to say now. There is no doubt that, at times of heavier shelling, there were more injuries. And when you have a large influx of the wounded, then their treatment takes 10, 12, or 15 hours. After that, it is possible that there would be a lull, but not necessarily. Sometimes we had to go on working until the lull came. So what I'm trying to say is that the shelling was not of the same intensity, and so that the number of wounded also varied accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Doctor, can you recall the longest kind of shift that you worked with your fellow surgeons in the hospital? How many hours at one time have you ever done treating patients?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think time passes quickly, you see. And one tends to forget the details and to suppress others. But I think that we worked hardest and for longest hours during the massacres in Sarajevo, and there were several of them. I think those were difficult times, not only for the injured but also for us who did our very best. We worked until exhaustion, certainly up to 15 hours without interruption. I have just remembered, in fact, you see, that the head of the surgical department in one such massacre set a record by operating continuously for 24 hours without interruption. That really is quite exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've just used the expression "massacres." Can you recall any particular times or dates that you would attribute that word to, and do you know anything about how they happened or what they were? Clearly, if you don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates. I just know that the first massacre occurred in the Vasa Miskin [phoen] Street. Vasa Miskin Street. It was described as a massacre in the media. Then there were massacres at marketplaces, Makali 1 and 2. And then in another part of the city near Dobrinja, there were several of those massacres. I was not in a position to follow all these things very closely, you see. Especially, I'm afraid I can't remember the dates. But you will find the dates registered in other services, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall, perhaps -- you've made reference to one specific street, Vasa Miskin. Do you know what the victims of that were supposed to have been doing at the time when they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning. They were waiting for bread to be distributed out of the humanitarian aid that had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you've also made a reference to "Makali 1." Do you recall even roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but in subsequent analyses and stories and judging by the influx of the injured, one could see that that part of the centre of town had probably been shelled. And judging by the injuries, the seriousness and the type of injury, one could see that they were the result of the devastating effect of shells and shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I would like to have a break. I don't know whether this is a good moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's a very good moment, Your Honour. I would like in a moment to play an excerpt of a videotape. My learned friends have the appropriate copy and so forth. It is a short clip, a minute or so, maybe, but it is germane to the evidence of this witness. Perhaps it could be a good time that we could see that immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's fine. Then we have a break for 20 minutes. We resume at 10 minutes to 6.00. Could you please bring the witness out of the courtroom; and Mr. Galic, you'll be guided out of the courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, when we had a break, you indicated that you would show a video. Do I understand, according to the rules that I pronounced earlier this day, that you will tender this video in evidence once all the parts have been played?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, essentially, that is a yes. But we are proposing a technical thing which might be more to the convenience of the Court at the end of the day. What we would like is if the -- at this stage, the clip that we show be marked for identification purposes. The idea of the Prosecution being that at the end of the day, when we have shown a number of the clips from the opening video to different witnesses, we would propose that they be placed on a DVD so that rather than individual cassettes being stacked up and handed in as a tendered exhibit, you would have one DVD OF all the sections that be marked, identified, and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as you state -- indicate that it would be practical to do otherwise, that those documents or videos that have been played already, they will be put on a list and they will be identified one of the coming days. So if it's part of it, I don't think it's necessary to provide us with an extra videotape. But as soon as you go out of the content of the video played, we would like to have it identified or at least know when with we can tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It is my intention today that we stick strictly to a portion of the tape that has been played already in that regard. I think my learned friend Mr. Ierace would like to address you on this particular issue a little further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution could appreciate some guidance in this regard. I anticipate that during the course of the Prosecution case, there will be a number of video clips that will be shown to various witnesses. Our concern is that if we did not take this compilation step, that ultimately there may be 20 or 30 videocassettes, each with a clip of only one or two minutes. Therefore, the proposal extends beyond the opening video. The idea we had in mind was that each of those clips could be marked for identification, and then at some convenient time, that could all be placed on either one video or a DVD, and then before each clip, there would be a text message stating which item it was by reference to the identification mark. If, however, the Trial Chamber would prefer that the clips were tendered separately, then of course we can do that starting with this one today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think -- first, has the Defence any opinion on the technicalities, any comments to make on the suggestions of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. You've taken me by surprise. I would have liked to have the opportunity to confer because though it is a good idea, we shouldn't -- it shouldn't produce results that would be not as good as we would wish. What may happen is that there may be parts in the whole tapes that may need to be replayed for other witnesses and not just clips, not just fragments. So I would suggest that we come back to this question later when we are -- as the Defence counsel -- when we have time to confer about this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we have to take a decision on the video clip to be played now at this moment. This is part of the video that has been played during the opening statement, so I would suggest -- I'll give you the opportunity perhaps to come back to it later. And I suggest that if you want whole video scenes, since these are just clips out of programmes, you perhaps communicate with the Prosecution whether you will be able to see the whole of the video programme, perhaps, of which it's taken out. And after you have discussed it with the Prosecution, to see whether you still need this to be in open court and have the video of which we only see a part to be played before the Court, or that you can just see whether there are any other parts of this video you would like to have played. And of course you can do that as Defence. You can tender into evidence whatever other individual video clips you want to. But for this moment, I would follow the suggestion of the Prosecution. That means that we will identify, give an identification number, for this clip to be played today, that it will be later part of a more extensive video CD -- DVD which will be tendered into evidence. And that it's not necessary at this moment, if it's given a proper name - and perhaps the Prosecution can invent a name for this clip of today - that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it's identified and later it will be tendered into evidence, and the parties will see whether there's any need of looking at the context of which the video is taken. If that will be acceptable to both parties, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you can come back later to your fundamental point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will indeed come back to the matter later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecution, any comment to make at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then could you please give a name to the clip you're going to play for us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. It is a clip relating to state hospital, so I would suggest, Your Honours, "State hospital - Mandilovic," which would then identify it to the witness, if that suits you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, we can't sign the clip at this moment. But it has received -- it has got this identification number. You may proceed, Mr. Blaxill

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Would you please bring in the witness, Mr. Usher. Please proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, at this stage I would be grateful if you would just view a short video clip that we will play to you, and then I will have just a few short questions to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I wonder if now the video clip could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That can be stopped now, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I noticed that the quality of the video now, which I presume is the same video as you showed to us during the opening statement, was for some technical reason of less quality. If it could be easily done, I would suggest that it be played again. It is just a short clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If that would show any improvement in the quality, then certainly we would do that. Otherwise, my learned friend and I were just discussing the potential of how to solve it. We could perhaps arrange with Your Honours, say, later on, on Monday, if this witness were still testifying, perhaps we could intervene in the course of cross-examination and show, hopefully, a cleaned-up copy. But if playing the clip one more time might help to resolve the issue right now, then indeed, we would be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, do you think that... I do understand that there are technical problems and it will not be possible to play the video in a better condition today. So I would suggest that the Prosecution be given the opportunity to play the video again next Monday. Of course, I don't know whether cross-examination has started already by then, but then we will slightly change the order and do it as soon as possible. Mr. Blaxill, then, perhaps without the video, so I assume that you will leave out a few questions as well, you may proceed as you would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged to Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Due to some technical problems, Dr. Mandilovic, I think we will move off the issue of the video for this moment. Doctor, could I ask you that during the time that we have been talking about, from late 1992 through to the middle of 1994, was there any military presence in the state hospital? By that, I mean the presence of any armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In the hospital, there was never any armed soldiers present. The soldiers that came to the hospital on any basis, whether they were injured and wounded or needing medical aid and assistance or whether they came to visit somebody who was sick in hospital, would always leave their weapons outside the hospital complex in a separate room designated for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, you have made reference to some people wounded by small-arms fire. Did small-arms fire ever actually hit the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think it did because all the windows on the hospital building were practically shattered. I don't know whether you can see it on the video clip. It is not precise enough, but on the better photographs, you can see that the entire south facade of the hospital, but the east one as well and partially the west, it was all bullet-riddled from small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did this bullet-riddling damage of the hospital, did that occur after September 1992 or continue after September 1992, and did it continue in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did it continue, in fact, through 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you give any idea to the Chamber as to where this small-arms fire came from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Following on from logics, the small-arms fire could only have come from the southeastern, southern, and southwestern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you attribute names of areas that were in those locations where you felt the fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise. I think it came from the slopes of the Trebevic mountain, the Jewish cemetery, and the Vrace part of Grbavica settlement, I think. Those are the zones which would correspond to the south-easterly, southern, and southwestern side, or the angles from which the firing could have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Doctor, were there ever occasions when shells landed or bullets struck as people were being admitted to the hospital? In other words, were people hit and wounded outside the hospital buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the hospital building itself, you couldn't hit a patient. You couldn't hit a person because the buildings that rise up in front of the hospital prevent a good angle of vision. You can't get a good view. So the injured who came to the hospital and were injured in front of the hospital, that was exclusively the result of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In your experience of being in Sarajevo, let alone being a surgeon at the hospital, which did you consider the greater hazard to people, the shelling or the sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Much greater danger was from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us why the one is so much more dangerous than the other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Because you could know approximately where a snipe-- sniper fire was coming from. And you would be able to protect yourself, to see that you weren't out in an open space facing the southern side. However, the projectiles of shells, you can't save yourself from projectiles of shells because they come in a parabola, in an arch, and are then dispersed and their destructive power is much greater than a bullet from a gunshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were any measures taken within the city, in fact, to give added protection to civilians from sniping, any form of --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Measures were undertaken at large crossroads open towards the south. They were protected with containers and metal barriers or screens. They were all improvised protection, but nonetheless quite good quality and good protection against sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Presumably, Doctor, such barriers were of no use against ammunition travelling in a parabola that you've just described, in other words, a shell falling into the city. They would offer no protection from that, would they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, they couldn't. You couldn't protect yourself from the parabola projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of this period from late September of 1992 to the first half of 1994, were there any casualties amongst patients who were actually wounded further whilst in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: There were several cases of wounding -- patients additionally wounded actually, patients and hospital staff. And because of that, we would lower the patients down as low as possible in the phases so that they would not be under sniper attack. I cannot say with any certainty how many. I'm sure those facts and figures existed and the hospital management probably has the information. But there must have been about ten all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in your experience in that hospital, I believe you made some mention of the relationship between the sort of military casualties you treated and the civilian. What can you say about the number of civilian casualties you observed in the city and how do you think so many, so many casualties could have been brought about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: What I think is the following: Sarajevo is a relatively large city with quite a large population, and you couldn't keep that entire population in a basement. The population had to move around. People went to work. They had to go and fetch foodstuffs or humanitarian aid. So the inhabitants had to move around over this long period of time. And when there was this movement on the part of the population, the inhabitants, any shell that fell had, following on from logics, to have wrought destruction because it is a town. There is concrete all around you, and wherever a shell falls leads to further dispersion and reverberation. And as I said a moment ago, it is very difficult when you are outside a basement or cellar to save yourself from that if there was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to be an explosion close by where you were. And it is precisely because of that that there were far more injured and wounded civilians coming into hospital. The soldiers were at the outskirts of town, and probably in trenches, too, so that they did have some protection, and there were fewer of them, fewer soldiers than there were civilians. So that is what led to this difference in percentages with respect to the wounded and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, can you please tell the Tribunal something of the emotional effects that the shelling and the sniping had upon people in Sarajevo, your observations perhaps of colleagues and patients and the population in general you had contact with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Over a long period of time, with the very difficult conditions of a state of siege with permanent shelling that was -- caused devastation, this must have had an effect on the mental makeup of man in such an environment. I personally think that in that -- at that stage, there was a particular fear, anxiety, all this gained particular expression, neurosis, neurasthenia, phobias of different kinds, all the deviant mental states and illnesses which were conditioned and the result of an unnatural state of affairs over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is there perhaps -- if I could ask sort of moving away from the slightly more medical approach, in just common parlance, could you sum up the mood of the people, how they felt on a daily basis undergoing life with the shelling and the sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: You know what it was like. First of all, you have the stage of fear. Then there's the phase of optimism when you think it will all pass. And when you see it doesn't pass, fear is multiplied and magnified with all its other repercussions and this would ultimately end in a pessimistic phase of indignation. So that ultimately, in the end, the population becomes completely blunt, if I can use that term, to everything going on around it. Numb, numb to everything going on around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you have any view or anything to say about the attacks on the hospital in relation to the mental effects upon the patients who were in that hospital at the time? Was there anything you noticed in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When there is fighting and when medical facilities are being attacked in war, this is particularly serious and has grave effects, not only on the hospital staff, and that is the essential point, but it has this effect on patients who experience once again trauma. So simplify matters, we have a doubling of traumatism, so you have somebody who is injured with a contusion, and he is in hospital, a place where he should be given peace and quiet, and he has to experience a repeated instance of a dangerous situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, did you have your family with you in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you say where they were living?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And your family consisted of whom, your wife and/or children?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, wife and child.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how did you feel on a daily basis with your family at the apartment and yourself working in the hospital; did this arouse any particular feelings in yourself, the shelling and sniping going on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to describe the states we were in. It was a state of permanent fear, not for your own personal safety but for your nearest and dearest, your family, your friends, your relatives, and the troubles aggravated because you were cut off -- you had no telephone link. If there was an attack, you couldn't ring up your apartment, your home, to ask how they were or what was going on. So that was an added aggravation. And it is very difficult to describe what one actually felt and what the situation was actually like after so much time, with this time distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, you've used the expression "the fear felt by people." As a layman, the word "fear" could mean any level of fear, from very small to very great. Can you put a level or just a word that would describe the degree of fear that was present in the population of Sarajevo when they were going through these months of shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's a very delicate question, subtle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to object to the question by my learned colleague in view of the specialist of the doctor. He is an ear, nose, and throat doctor, whereas my learned colleague has asked for the degree of fear. To assess the degree of fear, an assessment of the degree of fear is not within the domain of a doctor who is not a specialist in that realm, in that field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you respond to that, Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I will, Your Honour. Your Honour, a doctor is nonetheless the doctor. There is absolutely no effort by the Prosecution or indeed Dr. Mandilovic to represent himself in medical terms as a psychological or psychiatric expert. That is not our intent and we will certainly not go down that road. I think there are two aspects here that make it a relevant question. Firstly, as a doctor, he was treating a lot of people during the war. Doctors are professional people who will observe and have some knowledge of simple human experience. And the question I asked, I thought, was really directed simply at his observation of a level of fear he observed in people, or maybe even felt himself. And that can be, I think, even very much a layman's realm, because it is not that difficult for anyone with a degree of experience of life to see whether somebody appears to be calm or happy or very happy or ecstatically happy. We are asking simply for that, with the additional experience this man has brought to bear by having been a doctor treating people throughout that period but not beyond his general medical training, certainly not into the realms of specialty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the objection is denied. Dr. Mandilovic is not called as an expert on his medical specialty, and the question put to Dr. Mandilovic is such that it's asking for an assessment which can be made by any human being, so Dr. Mandilovic, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Fear as a form of human behaviour is difficult to level, to determine levels and degrees. Let me simplify matters, if I may. To all intents and purposes, you are living and working under constant fear. But the intensity of fear in different phases is different. That is to say, it increases or decreases. It is quite certain that when close by in your environment, several projectiles happen to hit, your fear multiplies and you then react in different ways. You react in a normal way, you panic, and so on and so forth. And in calm phases, the fear slowly subsides, is reduced in tension because ultimately, there is -- we cannot be in a state of permanent fear. And I said a moment ago that this is the stage where indignation steps in. I think that that is a very good expression to reflect the situation. One has exhausted the organism, the body. The mind is exhausted from permanent fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, thank you for that. I have really one further area to ask you briefly about, and again, I take note that I do not do so as if you are a psychologist or psychiatrist. I know that you are not, sir. But can you say something about any behaviour in people that has been noticed or has been manifest after the war? In other words, how are people today some years on? Are there any problems that still seem to persist mentally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there are certain repercussions in the present-day Sarajevo, especially among the people who spent the whole time in Sarajevo during the war. Those are my personal impressions. They need not be accurate. But I think that there is a significant percentage increase in various types of neurosis and neurasthenia among people in my immediate vicinity and beyond that, various illogical fears, the tendency to react stormily and unexpectedly, a high degree of intolerance and the like. There is no doubt that in addition to mental disorders, there are certain organic disorders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just have a moment, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours. I'm obliged, thank you, Dr. Mandilovic. Just remain there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Repeating that you'll have an opportunity to play the video next Monday, I would now give the Defence the opportunity to cross-examine Dr. Mandilovic. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence wishes to thank you, Mr. President. But before Ms. Pilipovic starts the cross-examination, I should like to raise a point which is in direct connection to the cross-examination. We should like to submit to the witness a document which is a document that has been disclosed by the Prosecution, not as an exhibit but among other documents. But it is not possible for me physically to find that exhibit among the binders that I mentioned the other day. I was able to find something on my computer, but the Defence does not have the ability to print this document. I can provide the references, but we can't print it. And if we wish to show it, we need to be able to produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find a practical solution. One moment, please. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you be in a position to copy the document you would like to show on a diskette, give it to the Registry, and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. usher will have it printed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can do, because I'm not a great expert, but I can give the references to the Prosecution, and then perhaps the Prosecution can do that because it is their document. I would be glad to do that. The reference, it is the following document: It is in the last list that I received. It is Document numbered 121002, and the number on the document itself is 00478801. Maybe I should repeat the numbers: 00478801. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question, did you indicate to the Prosecution that you wanted this document to be used during cross-examination or not? Perhaps we could have avoided all this delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for asking me that, but the documents that we will produce will always depend on what the witness says. And we never know in advance which documents we will need to produce. So I didn't have time to inform the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes you can foresee things that develop, because I would like to make quite clear that I would prefer not to lose any time on these practical problems during the Court hearing. So later we will be in a position to see whether this could have been prevented or not. But once again, I urge the parties to solve most of the practical problems out of this courtroom and not spending any time on it. But can the Prosecution produce the document on short notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. We have some people trying to obtain a copy of that document as I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, then, Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed in cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandilovic, good evening.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on the 11th of February, 2000, as a witness, you gave a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did make a statement, but I cannot confirm the date. I truly don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on the 5th of February, 2001, and on the 2nd of October, 2001, you had interviews with Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did have interviews with the investigators of the Tribunal, but I'm not certain about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started your testimony by saying that you arrived in Sarajevo when you were four years old. So you have been living in Sarajevo since 1953, together with your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was '53 or '54, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you moved to Sarajevo, and since then you have been permanently residing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you have been living and working in Sarajevo all this time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Responding to a question from my learned friend as to the situation in Sarajevo, you said it was difficult from the beginning of 1992 and that the situation gradually worsened. Could you explain what exactly you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that the situation was difficult at the beginning of 1992, I wasn't thinking of the wartime conditions. I was thinking of the general living conditions, that is, heightened political tensions in the town and in the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To be more specific, I'm going to ask you about the city of Sarajevo itself, as that is where you lived. You said that there were political tensions. Among whom were those tensions and at what level?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: When you have several parties, political parties, then there have to be tension. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that until then, relations in Sarajevo were harmonious and calm and that differences in views were not noticeable, nor that there were any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the multiparty system was established, the situation was far more stable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which were the political parties that were decisive in creating those difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The leading national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the formation of national parties was the cause of all the subsequent conflicts in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That's a political question, and now already a historical one. And I'm really not an expert for those matters, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that at the beginning of 1992, there were incidents and individual clashes. You said at the beginning of 1992 -- you didn't tell us exactly when, whether it was February, March, or April, but I assume that would be the beginning of 1992, you said that there were isolated clashes and incidents. Could you tell us which those incidents and conflicts were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to incidents and clashes on the political level. I personally was not involved in any such conflicts or incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were any actual physical conflicts in the course of the month of March in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In my surroundings, no, I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In what part of Sarajevo did you live as you were living in the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where the hospital is located.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality Centar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the conflict exploded on the 6th of April, and it started growing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- Dr. Mandilovic, I'd like to ask you, could you just look at your screen and wait until it stops moving before you give an answer, because the interpreters might not be able to follow it that quickly. But you understand each other, but it all has to be translated. Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you, and let me repeat, that that conflict climaxed on the 6th of April, and it gradually increased, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, at the beginning of April, there were various peace demonstrations all over town. Everybody wanted to be involved in the political game, to stand out. It is hard to say now, but I think already then, at the beginning of April, the situation gradually became abnormal, precisely because of those demonstrations, meetings in the assembly, in the centre of town, at Marijin Dvor. There were vast crowds of people waiting for something to be resolved. That's what I had in mind. It was an atmosphere that was out of the normal, out of the usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In April, you went regularly to work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether in the hospital in which you worked, were there any incidents? Were there any conflicts among certain people in the hospital, or was the situation normal as that was in those days a military hospital of the Yugoslav people's army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was as follows: Real conflicts of -- did not exist. The only thing that was noticeable in April was that Bosniak personnel were abandoning -- leaving the hospital and going home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why, if we just agreed that there were no incidents in the hospital itself? Why did Bosniak members of staff go home and leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: They left the hospital probably out of fear that there would be a repetition of the situation from Slavonija and Croatia, where wars had broken out. And I think that was the main reason for them to leave their working places.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But in the hospital itself, could you notice any manifestations of any particular feelings amongst staff with relation to people who you have described as Bosniak personnel? Was anyone giving them cause to fear a possible war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement which you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 11th of February, 2000, on page 4 of the B/C/S version, you said, "When the JNA withdrew from the state hospital, it was an organised departure and equipment and drugs were left behind. The hospital had been surrounded by patriotic forces and agreement had been reached that equipment would be left behind." Could you please tell us first when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, I did say that, but I didn't quite get your question. What exactly did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you when did this occur.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when the JNA left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, when the hospital was surrounded by patriotic forces and agreement had been reached that equipment would be left behind.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Let me see. Negotiations were conducted with the hospital management by entities from the city. I think the minister of the interior came and they negotiated how that should be done, in what manner. I played no part in that. I just know about it from hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the director of the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The director of the military hospital was Colonel Doctor Tomislav Dosan [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the minister participating in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The minister was Jusuf Pusina [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was the hospital surrounded by patriotic forces, and do you know who those patriotic forces were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I never saw those patriotic forces on the spot surrounding the hospital, but such an atmosphere was created in the hospital, and you had the impression that the hospital was in an encirclement. Probably that, with hindsight now, that was probably due to situations in Slavonija and Croatia where military facilities, including hospitals, were surrounded by certain civilian entities, and I think that could be ascribed to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak personnel that left the hospital as you said, did they do so before this event or after this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Which event?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the hospital was surrounded by patriotic forces and after the agreement had been reached, did the Bosniaks leave before or after?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak staff left consecutively, but I can't say that all of them left. That did not happen. They left gradually, individually, in the course of April. The agreement that I'm talking about, and which I remember, is the agreement that was reached, I think this was in May, just before the JNA staff left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that after a certain amount of time, the Bosniak staff members came back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the JNA staff had left, the Bosniak staff and others Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gradually started coming to the hospital. And they continued working as they did before they had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after this agreement was reached, the entire equipment and medicine -- medical supplies needed by the hospital were left behind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After that agreement was signed, were any changes made regarding the managerial staff of the hospital? You even told us that a new body was set up of which you were not a part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. After the JNA had left the hospital, the hospital continued working. For it to be able to work properly, it needed to have its management. And then in the first stage, we actually had a kind of triumvirate, to use that term, consisting of a Serb, a Croat, and a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the director of the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: It was a joint collective managerial body, and the operation or executive person was Doctor Bakanakas [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Had he worked in the hospital before then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he left the hospital and whether he left the hospital at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: He left the hospital sometime in April, but I don't know when. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in April 1992, there were individual shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: In April?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Will you tell me, please, which locations that you know of or remember were shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, according to the best -- my recollection, that most of the shooting occurred in the southern part of the city. I think this coincides -- I'm not quite certain, you see, but I think this coincided with certain battles over the police school at Vrace. That is the period. It is from that direction that considerable amount of shooting could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said battles between whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never there. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that in April, there was shelling and fighting in Ilidza, and that the hospital was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, which hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was the institute for physical therapy.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: The institute for physical therapy, I don't know that. I went there after the war, and I see that the institute was totally burned down. But when it was burned down, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents within the framework of the conflict in the city of Sarajevo that stood out in the course of the month of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Already in May, there was a lot of firing around town. I remember that well. And in town, itself, the situation was difficult. It was a state problem. I think this was on the 2nd or the 3rd of May, 1992 when the incident occurred with President Izetbegovic, and when that bad situation occurred with the command of the military district and there was some sort of an exchange and so on. But I know this from the media. All this was beyond my immediate surroundings and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you working in the military hospital at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I left the military hospital on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Of that same year, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you go back?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the 14th, 15th, or 16th? Those were hard times. But in any event, in the second half of the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to leave the hospital on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, did I have to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did. But I didn't have to. No one forced me out. No one pointed a gun at me and told me to go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't mean that. I just wanted you to explain for me the period when you were not in hospital, because you told me that you had worked at the hospital throughout.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I did, with the exception of those ten days or so. With the exception of those ten or so days, then I did work in the hospital all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you on annual leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: No, you must be joking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, just please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you anything you ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we are close to 7.00 by now. Could you please give us an estimate on how much time do you think you still need for the cross-examination? That's my first question. And my second question is whether you could find a proper moment within the next two or three minutes to, for today, finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my cross-examination will take another hour and a half, and I think that this is a good time for us to interrupt the cross-examination and resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. We adjourn these proceedings until Monday. We'll start at 9.00 in the morning and we'll continue until 1.45 p.m. And then I would like to ask the usher to bring the witness out of the courtroom. There's another question, Mr. Ierace, as far as I understand, but it's not necessary for the witness to attend. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you know that you have to pre-number it according to your system if you tender the document in evidence.
